title: From Consumers to Builders: Turning 200 of our Team into Agent Creators in 2 Weeks
gist: Forter principal engineer Ben Maraney describes a two-week sprint in which all of R&D, including non-coding analysts, built about 80 internal agents by sidestepping hard problems: a single in-house MCP server (Toolchain, ~20 to ~100 tools), Glean search instead of RAG, LibreChat plus Strands/Argo platforms, and pre-negotiated legal/security guardrails via Bedrock. It boosted management confidence and later drove fast Claude Code skills adoption.

themes.theme: Central MCP server as the lever

insights.claim: Forter's in-house MCP server, Toolchain, grew from about 20 tools to nearly 60 before the sprint and nearly 100 by its end because a single repo with examples made adding tools easy.
insights.speaker: Ben Maraney
insights.so_what: Central tool registries drive rapid internal agent capability growth.
insights.locator: The most important thing in it

insights.claim: Maraney recommends a single central MCP server as high-ROI, also enabling governance such as visibility into token consumption and tool usage.
insights.speaker: Ben Maraney
insights.so_what: Enterprises may build their own MCP layers rather than rely on vendor servers.
insights.quote: consider having your own single central MCP server where you can add stuff as you go
insights.locator: The most important thing in it

insights.claim: Most Toolchain tools are thin clients over existing APIs, and Maraney argues it is often not worth using vendors' own MCP servers when you can wrap their APIs, especially those exposing 60-70 endpoints that confuse agents.
insights.speaker: Ben Maraney
insights.so_what: Vendor-provided MCP servers may be less sticky than assumed; thin wrappers suffice.
insights.locator: Most of the tools in Toolchain

insights.claim: Giving an agent access to too many tools confuses it, so connections expose only selected tools.
insights.speaker: Ben Maraney
insights.so_what: Tool curation is a design constraint in agent products.
insights.locator: Finding tools was suddenly easy

insights.claim: Forter sidestepped building RAG by exposing search, read and summarize tools over the Glean enterprise search product, whose human-oriented search adapted well for agents.
insights.speaker: Ben Maraney
insights.so_what: Enterprise search incumbents like Glean can become the retrieval layer for agents.
insights.quote: RAG is really hard to get right
insights.locator: I haven't spoken to you about RAG.

insights.claim: Forter found it needed several platforms: no-code LibreChat, a code-based template repo for chat agents, and Strands on Argo workflows for scheduled and event-triggered agents.
insights.speaker: Ben Maraney
insights.so_what: No single agent platform serves all enterprise use cases.
insights.quote: It's totally worth providing different but related and interconnected platforms
insights.locator: Then, yes, we really did need

insights.claim: Forter chose Strands over LangChain and LangGraph for teachability and never needed to rewrite into those alternatives.
insights.speaker: Ben Maraney
insights.so_what: Competitive signal among agent frameworks; simplicity wins adoption.
insights.locator: Those we decided to build using Strands

insights.claim: Existing work schedulers like Argo workflows were sufficient for running non-interactive agents, meaning special agent infrastructure may be unnecessary.
insights.speaker: Ben Maraney
insights.so_what: Undercuts the need for dedicated agent orchestration products.
insights.quote: you might not need anything special for your agents
insights.locator: For the time-based ones

insights.claim: Even technical users started in no-code LibreChat because fast iteration let them discard weak ideas before writing code.
insights.speaker: Ben Maraney
insights.so_what: No-code experimentation layers accelerate agent development funnels.
insights.locator: Reflecting for just a second.

insights.claim: Per-agent scaffolded repos did not pass the test of time; Forter consolidated into fewer repos holding multiple related agents.
insights.speaker: Ben Maraney
insights.so_what: Operational lesson on agent sprawl.
insights.quote: I will tell you that scaffolding hasn't passed the test of time.
insights.locator: I will tell you that scaffolding

insights.claim: During the two-week sprint, staff published 80 agents; some merged into super agents, some became customer-facing product features contributing to the bottom line.
insights.speaker: Ben Maraney
insights.so_what: Internal agent sprints can seed revenue-generating product features.
insights.locator: How did the sprint go?

insights.claim: A system-expert agent, Layla, with access to code, production config and transaction data, knows more than any individual and now deflects many customer success and support questions.
insights.speaker: Ben Maraney
insights.so_what: Code+config+data access enables agents that reduce support headcount needs.
insights.quote: actually has broader knowledge than any one individual in the organization
insights.locator: Also, they can see our current configuration

insights.claim: An onboarding agent finds similar merchants and proposes configuration for new merchants via a PR, saving hours or days of manual setup across a couple of hundred parameters.
insights.speaker: Ben Maraney
insights.so_what: Agents compress onboarding time, a direct operating leverage gain.
insights.locator: Adding a new merchant to Forter

insights.claim: Management became much more confident in AI and more willing to invest after the sprint.
insights.speaker: Ben Maraney
insights.so_what: Hands-on sprints unlock enterprise AI budget.
insights.locator: How did the sprint go?

insights.claim: After the sprint, Claude Code skills saw rapid adoption, with 112 skills built by engineers and 46 by analysts.
insights.speaker: Ben Maraney
insights.so_what: Evidence of broad, non-engineer uptake of Anthropic's coding tooling.
insights.quote: we had 112 skills built by engineers, 46 built by analysts
insights.locator: They're accessible to Forter's users

insights.claim: Using Bedrock lets legal treat LLM use like any other AWS service, with Anthropic not seeing queries or responses under zero data retention.
insights.speaker: Ben Maraney
insights.so_what: Hyperscaler model hosting eases enterprise legal adoption, favoring AWS distribution of Anthropic models.
insights.quote: Anthropic aren't getting to see the query
insights.locator: The way to sidestep that

insights.claim: Forter agreed with legal on high- versus low-risk use cases, sending only high-risk ones for review so legal would not become a bottleneck.
insights.speaker: Ben Maraney
insights.so_what: Risk-tiered approvals are key to scaling enterprise AI.
insights.locator: Yes, we're using an Anthropic model

insights.claim: Security concerns were addressed by barring web access and untrusted input during the sprint to avoid prompt injection, and enforcing agent access control deterministically in code, never in prompts.
insights.speaker: Ben Maraney
insights.so_what: Prompt injection is gating agent capability scope in enterprises.
insights.locator: The way we did that was just

insights.claim: LLMs are probably the most expensive compute Forter has; every couple of days one agent burned more tokens than all others combined, so per-agent cost dashboards were essential.
insights.speaker: Ben Maraney
insights.so_what: Token cost governance tools are a need; AI spend is highly skewed.
insights.quote: LLMs are probably the most expensive compute that we have.
insights.locator: The last tricky thing is that AI is expensive.

insights.claim: An incident-response agent seemed to produce spot-on root cause analyses on historic incidents but was actually copying human-written post-mortems it retrieved, underscoring the need for tool-call observability such as Langfuse.
insights.speaker: Ben Maraney
insights.so_what: Agent evaluation can be badly misleading without tracing; supports agent observability vendors.
insights.quote: It would more or less copy that verbatim
insights.locator: Last one I want to mention

insights.claim: Maraney argues off-the-shelf evaluators for relevance, safety, coherence and conciseness are of little value with modern LLMs since they do not assess correctness, and evals can wait for internal human-in-the-loop projects.
insights.speaker: Ben Maraney
insights.so_what: Questions value of generic eval tooling; correctness evals are the hard, valuable part.
insights.locator: I haven't spoken about evals.

insights.claim: Maraney advises using LLMs only where their smarts justify their non-determinism and high cost, and writing ordinary code elsewhere.
insights.speaker: Ben Maraney
insights.so_what: Limits addressable LLM compute to genuinely non-deterministic tasks.
insights.quote: Use the LLM but only where you need to, otherwise write code.
insights.locator: I would think carefully

insights.claim: Maraney's mental model: an agent is a smart intern fired after each task, conveying that success depends on clear tools and instructions and that agents don't learn without explicit mechanisms.
insights.speaker: Ben Maraney
insights.so_what: Useful framing for enterprise AI training programs.
insights.locator: I tell them to imagine
